description: SkyShift Murcia is a team of five from Murcia, Spain, working on the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge: Teo (data and pipeline), Pedro (web), Antonio (presentation and submission), Benjamín (science of motion) and Juan (science of brightness and quality checks). We built SkyShift so that anyone can watch the infrared sky move, using open NASA SPHEREx data.
summary: SkyShift lets anyone watch the infrared sky move. Pick a star, type coordinates or click anywhere on the map: SkyShift fetches every NASA SPHEREx image of that spot from IRSA, keeps those taken at the same wavelength, aligns them and plays them as a time-lapse, so moving objects jump out and variable stars flicker. It goes beyond viewing. It stacks each visit to reveal objects too faint for a single image (the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855 appears at signal-to-noise 17.7), subtracts dates so only movers remain, draws infrared spectra from all six SPHEREx detectors, even on the fly for any point, and shows each detector separately so real motion can be told apart from defects. We tested it on the five challenge objects: for Barnard's Star we measure 11.5 ± 1.1″/yr, against 10.4″/yr from ESA's Gaia DR3. Everything SkyShift flags is a candidate, and anyone can report one and discuss it in public. SkyShift turns an expert archive into a place where curious people can help find the Sun's hidden neighbours.
details:
Try it in two minutes

WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf: invisible in single SPHEREx images, it appears when each visit is stacked. https://skyshift-roan.vercel.app/?object=wise-0855-stacked

Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in our sky: press "Watch it move", then compare its motion with Gaia DR3. https://skyshift-roan.vercel.app/?object=barnard

Epsilon Indi B in Science mode: the Difference view leaves only the mover, and the Bands tab shows the same motion in four detectors. https://skyshift-roan.vercel.app/?mode=science&object=eps-indi-b

UX Orionis: a young star whose brightness changes between visits. https://skyshift-roan.vercel.app/?object=ux-orionis

If NASA's IRSA archive is down (it was for most of the hackathon weekend), the guided tour still works, because its data are stored in our repository.

What it does

SkyShift is a free, public web tool that lets anyone see how the infrared sky changes over time, using data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Open the all-sky SPHEREx map, move freely, type the name of an object or click any point of the sky: SkyShift fetches every SPHEREx image of that spot and plays them as a time-lapse. Guided tours show the five challenge test objects (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis) plus UX Orionis as an extra. Free navigation and guided tours were ideas from our team, so that people without any astronomy background can explore without knowing coordinates.

How we use NASA data

Every image in SkyShift comes from NASA's SPHEREx mission, through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). For any point of the sky, SkyShift asks IRSA which SPHEREx images cover it, downloads small cutouts, reads the exact wavelength at that spot from each image's WCS-WAVE layer and keeps only images of similar wavelength (within 2%), so we compare like with like. It subtracts the zodiacal light, aligns every image on a common sky grid and plays them in date order. Each frame shows the SPHEREx quality flags, decoded from the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement. For the challenge test objects we go further: we measure positions and compare them with the catalogue proper motion; we stack all images of each visit, which reveals WISE 0855 (invisible in a single image, signal-to-noise about 18 when stacked); we subtract the first visit from the last, so still sources cancel out and moving ones leave a before/after pair; and we build infrared spectra from 0.75 to 5 microns using all six SPHEREx detectors. We are honest about the limits: Barnard's Star and R Draconis saturate the detector, SPHEREx visits a given spot only about every six months, and every result is presented as a candidate. All code is open (MIT) and reproducible in pipeline/.

What the user sees

A time-lapse player with dates and quality flags; a Difference view where only moving objects remain, as a blue (first visit) and red (last visit) pair; a position-versus-time chart compared with the catalogue motion; a brightness-versus-time chart for the variable stars; and an infrared spectrum panel. A Bands tab shows each SPHEREx detector (D1 to D6) alone or added, with the motion measured in each. Every object and candidate has a Discuss button that opens a GitHub Discussions thread, and anyone can send a new candidate with Report a candidate. Positions are validated against ESA's Gaia DR3: SPHEREx gives 11.5 ± 1.1″/yr for Barnard's Star, Gaia DR3 gives 10.4″/yr, and Epsilon Indi B moves the same way in four detectors. A Spectrum tab draws the infrared spectrum of any clicked point on the fly, and a False colour view shows three infrared bands as red, green and blue, so the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855 stands out in red next to bluer background stars; its brightness is compared with the clean NEOWISE W2 value (see What we measured).

What we measured

Barnard's Star: 11.5 ± 1.1″/yr in declination from SPHEREx, against 10.4″/yr from Gaia DR3.

WISE 0855: −10.9 ± 2.0″/yr in right ascension from three stacked visits, against −8.1″/yr in the catalogue. Its 4-5 µm brightness, 535 ± 27 µJy, is 14 % above the clean NEOWISE value (Wright & Foley 2025), as expected from a background star next to it.

Epsilon Indi B: the same shift in four detectors. Declination agrees with the catalogue; right ascension is about 2.5 standard errors low, which we report openly (short baseline, 6″ pixels, two brown dwarfs blended into one point).

These agree with the catalogues within the precision that a year and a half of 6″ SPHEREx pixels allows.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

SPHEREx maps the whole sky again and again, but its archive is built for experts. SkyShift turns it into something citizen scientists, students and curious people can use in a few clicks, following the example of WiseView, which the challenge suggests as inspiration. Today anyone can report a candidate and discuss it with amateurs and scientists. Next steps: the whole SPHEREx sky, voting on candidates, and automatic ranking of the most promising movers, to help the hunt for worlds like Planet X.

Tools

Data pipeline: Python with astropy, astroquery, reproject, numpy and matplotlib. Web: JavaScript, React, Vite and Aladin Lite v3, hosted on Vercel, with a small serverless function that acts as a bridge to IRSA (browsers cannot call IRSA directly). Code: https://github.com/teoaguiilar/skyshift. All sources are listed in SOURCES.md. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant for coding, data analysis, translation and the video script, ElevenLabs for the AI-generated voiceover of the demo video, and Higgsfield (GPT Image) for the five AI-generated cartoon presenters in the video, labelled "AI-generated characters" on screen; every use is listed in AI_USAGE.md. The ideas and decisions are the team's.
